analysis.one_liner: Lets the government negotiate Medicare prescription drug prices directly with manufacturers.
analysis.headline: The bill drew 175 cosponsors from both parties but never got a vote, dying in House health subcommittees.
analysis.plain_summary: The 2003 Medicare drug benefit law barred the government from negotiating drug prices with manufacturers. This bill repealed that ban and gave the Health and Human Services Secretary the same bargaining power the VA and Defense Department already use to buy drugs in bulk, with the goal of getting seniors the lowest possible price. It was referred to two House committees and their health subcommittees, where it sat until Congress ended without ever coming up for a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Medicare beneficiaries, who would pay lower out-of-pocket drug costs if the government could bargain prices down, and taxpayers, who help fund Medicare's drug benefit and would benefit from lower reimbursement prices.

how_it_helps.text: The bill strikes the 'noninterference' provision added by the 2003 Medicare drug law, which prohibited the Secretary of Health and Human Services from interfering in negotiations between drug manufacturers and pharmacies or plan sponsors, and from requiring particular formulary pricing.

In its place, the Secretary would have authority similar to that of the Secretary of Veterans Affairs and Secretary of Defense to negotiate contracts with manufacturers of covered Medicare Part D drugs, with the stated goal of ensuring beneficiaries pay the lowest possible price.

analysis.who_pays: Brand-name drug manufacturers, who would face a single very large buyer bargaining prices down across the entire Medicare Part D market — the same bargaining pressure they already face from the VA and Pentagon, which buy drugs at lower negotiated rates.

drawbacks.text: The noninterference ban the bill repealed was written to keep the government from steering the market: opponents argued that federal negotiating power could effectively require formularies to impose price structures and could steer patients away from some drugs, reducing access to certain medicines even as prices fall.
Manufacturers and free-market critics contended that letting the government negotiate would squeeze industry revenue and, over time, reduce the returns that fund research into new drugs.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For seniors and taxpayers the upside is large: Medicare is the biggest drug buyer in the country, and the VA and Defense Department already buy the same drugs at negotiated discounts. The main honest cost is the risk that a powerful government buyer limits which drugs are covered or slows future drug development by compressing manufacturer profits. The bill offered no concrete mechanism beyond broad negotiating authority, so its real-world effect would have depended heavily on how a given administration used it.

outcome.mechanism: The House referred it to the Energy and Commerce and Ways and Means committees, each sent it to its health subcommittee, and it stayed there until the 108th Congress ended with no hearing, no markup, and no floor vote.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced January 20, 2004, by Rep. Dennis Moore with a bipartisan group of original cosponsors including Reps. Emerson (R), Davis (D), Burton (R), Emanuel (D), and Wamp (R).
It was referred to both the Energy and Commerce Committee and the Ways and Means Committee on the day of introduction, meaning both committees had to act before the bill could reach the floor.
Within days, each committee referred the bill to its Subcommittee on Health, the standard holding pen for Medicare legislation, where no further action was taken.
By the end of the Congress it had 175 cosponsors — 154 Democrats, 20 Republicans, and 1 independent — but the bill never received a committee markup or a floor vote in either chamber.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Pharmaceutical manufacturers, who kept the legal ban on Medicare price negotiation intact; that ban remained the law for years afterward, preserving the industry's pricing power over the largest drug-buying program in the country.

for.name: Rep. Dennis Moore
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to repeal the ban on Medicare drug price negotiation and give the HHS Secretary bargaining authority like the VA's.

for.name: 154 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, the overwhelming majority of its support.

for.name: 20 House Republicans and 1 independent
for.what_they_did: Joined Democrats in cosponsoring, giving the bill bipartisan backing.

against.name: House committee leadership
against.role: Chairs of the Energy and Commerce and Ways and Means committees
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for a committee vote; it was referred to the health subcommittees and no markup or hearing followed.

against.name: Presidential administration
against.role: President George W. Bush and his administration
against.what_they_did: Fought to preserve the noninterference clause in the 2003 Medicare drug law and opposed giving the government authority to negotiate drug prices, making the bill's core provision a nonstarter with the committee leadership.

sides.party_line_note: Cosponsorship was bipartisan — 154 Democrats, 20 Republicans, and 1 independent — but every gatekeeping step that killed the bill sat in the hands of the Republican House leadership, and no vote was ever allowed.

industries.note: The bill would have stripped the ban on Medicare price negotiation, exposing the industry's largest single market to the same bulk-purchasing bargaining the VA and Pentagon already use to pay less for the same drugs. Keeping the ban preserved manufacturer pricing power at the expense of seniors' drug costs.

industries.industry: Prescription drug plans and pharmacy benefit managers
industries.note: The bill repealed the noninterference language protecting the private plans and intermediaries that run Part D pricing, and removed the ban on the Secretary requiring particular formulary price structures. It would have shifted pricing leverage from these private intermediaries to the federal government.
